prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

That this mountainside looks like a face is accidental, which is a shame, for I dearly love to laugh. The touch-smoothed redwood cross-section, in its rings of growth and brightness, seems like a sun seen from underwater, wobbly as jelly, mocking my inability to find a job, my food stamps, and saddens me to see the teens tagging themselves in nearby places to earn a virtual friend's respect, or boasting other symptoms of youth while leaving their greasy fingerprints on the thick lenses of my glasses, mocking my desire for artwork to remain packed in straw, and in music for sleepers halfway awake to grow wild in. It all gives me faith in arranging, I guess, when there is nothing else I seem much good at but fuss and copy and paste, with a head full of so many other worries. Got a check today. Bought a book I can't read without it putting me to sleep with its out-of-date luxuriousness. So instead of reading it, I stayed up and listened to Harry Partch's songAnd on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma, dedicating it to the memory of Ramon Novarro, hoping it would arch electrically above him with all the characteristics of fire all night, all day, and soak his early spring colors in a late autumn sun as pale as silver and fern-green skiesto draw light through midnight

outputs.L1:
That this mountainside resembles a face is purely accidental—which is a shame, for I dearly love to laugh. The touch-smoothed redwood cross-section, with its rings of growth and brightness, resembles a sun seen from underwater, wobbling like jelly and mocking my inability to find a job and my reliance on food stamps. It saddens me to see teenagers tagging themselves in nearby places to earn a virtual friend’s respect, or displaying other symptoms of youth while leaving greasy fingerprints on the thick lenses of my glasses, mocking my desire for artwork to remain packed in straw and for music in which half-awake sleepers might grow wild.

All of this gives me faith in arranging, I suppose, when there seems to be little else I am good at beyond fussing, copying, and pasting, my head crowded with so many other worries. I received a check today and bought a book I cannot read without being lulled to sleep by its out-of-date luxuriousness. So, instead of reading it, I stayed up and listened to Harry Partch’s song *And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma*, dedicating it to the memory of Ramon Novarro and hoping it would arch electrically above him, bearing all the characteristics of fire, all night and all day, and soak his early-spring colors in a late-autumn sun, beneath skies as pale as silver and fern-green, drawing light through midnight.
outputs.L2: The resemblance between this slope and a human face is pure coincidence—unfortunate, since laughter is something I cherish. Polished by countless hands, the redwood cross-section, with its luminous growth rings, resembles a sun viewed beneath water, trembling like gelatin. It seems to ridicule my unemployment and dependence on food stamps. I am also disheartened by teenagers tagging nearby surfaces to win the approval of online friends, or displaying other signs of adolescence while smearing oily fingerprints across the heavy lenses of my glasses. All of this mocks my wish that art might stay cushioned in straw and that music might offer a place where half-awake sleepers can flourish untamed. Still, I suppose it strengthens my belief in arranging things, because little else seems to suit me beyond fretting, copying, and pasting while countless anxieties crowd my mind. A check arrived today. I used it to buy a book whose dated opulence sends me to sleep whenever I try to read it. Rather than open it, I remained awake listening to Harry Partch’s *And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma*. I dedicated the piece to Ramon Novarro’s memory, imagining it curving electrically over him, endowed with every quality of fire through night and day, saturating his early-spring colors in the pale silver light of a late-autumn sun and fern-green skies, drawing brightness through midnight.

outputs.L4:
I was unemployed then, and worry had become the ordinary climate of my days. Each morning brought the same questions: how long the money would last, whether another letter of refusal was waiting, whether my work had any value beyond the private need that produced it. The city seemed to move without me. People hurried toward offices, appointments, and obligations, while I drifted among them, watching from the margins and feeling both exposed and invisible.

Yet beauty kept interrupting my anxiety. It appeared accidentally—in sunlight striking a window, in a bright scrap of color on the pavement, in the momentary arrangement of strangers at a crossing. None of these impressions offered comfort in any deliberate way. They simply existed, vivid and complete, indifferent to my circumstances. Because I could not control my life, I began arranging what I saw: colors, gestures, overheard phrases, memories, and passing faces. Making patterns from them became a modest form of survival.

I tried to read, hoping a book might impose order on the day, but the words would not hold still. I turned the pages without entering them. The sentences remained distant, sealed behind the pressure of my own thoughts, and at last I put the book aside. My failure to read felt like another symptom of my failure to work, to belong, to make anything coherent. Then I put on music by Harry Partch.

The first sounds altered the room. Partch’s strange instruments and intervals did not resemble the familiar language from which I already felt excluded. The music seemed built from another scale of attention—physical, ceremonial, almost architectural. Its tones made space around themselves. Instead of asking me to understand, they asked me to listen.

As I listened, I thought of Ramon Novarro: the beautiful face preserved by film, the radiance of an earlier world, and the brutality that ended his life. The music became, in my mind, a memorial for him—not a formal elegy, but an imagined rite. Novarro’s image moved through the metallic resonances and unexpected harmonies, no longer merely a relic of glamour or a victim recalled through scandal. He became a figure of fragile beauty carried forward by sound.

My private fears did not disappear. I was still unemployed; the future remained uncertain; the work I wanted to make still seemed beyond my abilities. But the music changed the scale of those worries. It gathered them into something larger, where grief, beauty, humiliation, and desire could exist together without canceling one another. What had seemed like useless distraction—the light on glass, the accidental colors, the remembered face—became material for imagination.

I began to see an inward procession of light and color: gold flaring against darkness, deep reds and blues unfolding like banners, faces emerging and receding. The vision was not an escape from loss but a way of carrying loss without surrendering to it. Beauty endured not because it was safe, but because it could be rediscovered, rearranged, and made present again.

When the music ended, the room was the same, and so was my life. Still, I no longer felt entirely abandoned to anxiety. Listening had become an act of creation, and remembrance had become a form of faith. I could not know whether I would find work or make the art I imagined, but I could still attend to the world. I could gather its scattered brightness and trust that, through patience and invention, it might continue to shine.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single stream-of-consciousness prose poem about unemployment, art, aging, and insomnia, incorporating a face-shaped mountainside, a polished redwood cross-section, food stamps, teenage vandals, Harry Partch, and Ramon Novarro.
counterfactuals.output: At four in the morning unemployment sits on my chest like a patient animal, breathing for both of us, while the refrigerator hums its one-note opera and the food stamps curl beside the grocery list, small blue permissions to continue; I think of art, how it keeps asking for materials when time itself has become expensive, and of the polished redwood cross-section hanging above my desk, its rings varnished into amber weather, each year narrowed or widened by conditions the tree could neither negotiate nor escape, which is perhaps aging, which is perhaps labor, which is perhaps why my face in the darkened window resembles that face-shaped mountainside outside town, brow of granite, mouth broken open by frost, staring upward as if sleep were a star it had been promised. Teenage vandals spray-painted silver teeth along its lower cliff last summer, and everyone called it desecration, though I secretly admired their insomnia, their ladders, their reckless need to sign the ancient; somewhere Harry Partch is building an instrument from salvage and naming every impossible interval, somewhere Ramon Novarro remains young in a silent frame while the actor himself moves toward the terrible knowledge waiting beyond the screen, and I, résumé revised again, count the redwood’s rings as if they were coins, as if one could purchase another decade, another dream, another hour without the ceiling’s blank face. Morning will come and call itself opportunity, wearing the cheap tie of daylight, and I will rise because hunger is a metronome, because beauty is not employment but it keeps irregular hours, because even the mountain with its ruined painted mouth seems about to speak, though all it says is endure, endure, endure, in a voice too low for sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental literary collage in the style of a disjointed diary entry. Use long, winding sentences, surreal visual metaphors, abrupt personal confessions, and end with an image of light passing through midnight.
counterfactuals.output:
**17 October, or possibly the inside of a blue cup**

This morning arrived sideways, dragging its wet hem through the apartment, and I watched the windows fill with pale buildings that seemed to have been folded from old receipts, each one trembling with the arithmetic of lives I will never enter, while on the table the pear darkened quietly beside a spoon, as if the two had made an agreement not to mention me.

I dreamed my mother was a hotel with no doors.  
I have not called her in eleven days.

At noon, the city opened its mechanical mouth and swallowed three buses, a flock of umbrellas, the small red glove of a child, and all my good intentions, which were tied together with dental floss and labeled **FOR LATER**, though later is only a corridor where the wallpaper remembers being trees.

*

There was a horse in the elevator.

No one else appeared surprised.

It wore rain in its mane and looked at me with the exhausted tenderness of someone who has read every letter I never sent; when the doors opened on the seventh floor, it stepped out into Accounting, leaving behind the smell of grass and thunderstorms, and I wanted to follow, but I was afraid they would ask for identification.

Confession: I steal sugar packets from cafés.  
Confession: sometimes I hold them in my pockets and imagine I am carrying small white winters.  
Confession: I lied when I said I was fine. It was easier than describing the cathedral collapsing inside my left shoe.

The afternoon stretched itself across the hours like a cat made of smoke, knocking over names, dates, a glass of water, the face I wore in 2019, and somewhere a telephone kept ringing beneath the floorboards, perhaps for me, perhaps for the woman who lived here before and left a single black button in the medicine cabinet, smooth as a closed eye.

**Note to self:** buy bread, batteries, courage.  
**Another note:** stop making lists of impossible groceries.

By evening, the walls had moved closer, though politely, and I sat between them listening to the refrigerator hum its one frozen syllable while the moon hung above the fire escape like a fingernail clipped from some enormous sleeping god; I thought of everyone I have loved badly, which is not the same as not loving them, and of everyone who loved me with both hands while I stood there pretending to be weather.

I miss you.  
There.  
The sentence is out, crawling across the page with its soft, embarrassing legs.

Near midnight I went to the roof, where the antennas stitched and unstitched the sky, and the streets below shone black as spilled film, each car carrying a private apocalypse toward the river, each apartment window a tiny aquarium of grief, dinner, television, forgiveness; then the clouds broke without sound, and one thin beam crossed the darkness—not banishing it, not explaining anything—only passing, impossibly tender, like light threading a needle through midnight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a melancholy but darkly comic monologue by an unemployed artist who visits a museum, worries about money, buys an unreadable old-fashioned book, and stays awake listening to Harry Partch’s “And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma.”
counterfactuals.output:
I went to the museum because it was free, which is the unemployed person’s preferred school of aesthetics.

At the entrance, a glass box invited donations. I put in a button. Not intentionally—I was searching my pocket for a coin, found none, and the button came off my coat in protest. It lay there among the five-dollar bills looking like a tiny portrait of my financial situation.

Inside, I stood before a large abstract painting: three black bars, a red wound, and a yellow square apparently trying to leave. According to the label, it concerned “the failure of industrial optimism.” I understood it immediately. Industrial optimism and I had recently stopped speaking.

I am an artist, although at present the economy has relieved me of the burden of proving it. My paintings lean against the wall of my apartment with the patient accusation of unpaid witnesses. Every morning I tell them, “Today we find a gallery.” Every evening we eat pasta without sauce.

At the museum café, a sandwich cost fourteen dollars. I studied it from a respectful distance. It appeared to contain arugula and private health insurance.

Instead, I went to the gift shop, where despair is available in several tasteful formats. I could not afford a postcard, but next door there was a used-book stall, and because poverty makes philosophers of us all, I spent my last eight dollars on a crumbling volume called *The Moral Architecture of the Celestial Spheres*, printed in 1873 in a typeface designed to keep knowledge from the lower classes.

I carried it home like stolen fire.

That night I tried to read it. The author began with a sentence containing “wherefore,” two semicolons, and a reference to a duke whose principal achievement seemed to be having opinions in Latin. By page three, I had learned that the universe was a staircase, God was an architect, and women were probably curtains.

I closed the book.

Then I checked my bank account again, in case money had entered it through a clerical miracle. It had not. The balance was so low it looked less like a number than a temperature at which pipes burst.

I lay awake and listened to Harry Partch’s *And on the Seventh Day Petals Fell in Petaluma*. Strange, beautiful instruments knocked and shimmered in the dark. The music sounded like a civilization assembling itself out of driftwood, hubcaps, and the bones of extinct furniture. Every note seemed both discovered and slightly illegal.

At three in the morning, I began to feel hopeful, which was irritating.

Perhaps because Partch had built his own instruments, his own tuning, his own peculiar country of sound. He had looked at the official world—with its approved scales, salaried experts, and sandwiches priced like minor surgeries—and said, no, thank you, I’ll construct another one.

So I got out of bed and stood among my unsold paintings.

They looked different in the streetlight. Not better, exactly. But loyal.

Tomorrow, I decided, I would make something new. Something impractical and difficult and possibly unreadable. Something no one had requested.

After all, I already owned the book.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn these ideas into one dense surreal paragraph: accidental faces in nature, a redwood slab like an underwater sun, joblessness and food stamps, teenagers seeking online approval, fingerprints on glasses, arranging and copying as artistic practice, an unexpected check, insomnia, Ramon Novarro, and electrically arcing music.
counterfactuals.output: Faces kept accidentally surfacing in the bark, the clouds, the bruised skin of fruit, while a redwood slab hung in the room like an underwater sun, drowning everything in amber rings; jobless, awake for the third night, living on food stamps and the rumor of an unexpected check, I watched teenagers tilt their bright faces toward the tribunal of online approval, each heart-click flashing like a tiny verdict, and wiped fingerprints from glasses only to discover new constellations in the grease. Arranging and copying became my artistic practice—chair beside shadow, receipt beside leaf, Ramon Novarro’s impossible profile beside the refrigerator’s blue hum—until the apartment seemed less composed than counterfeited, every object rehearsing another object’s dream, and somewhere behind the walls music began electrically arcing from note to note, a radiant short circuit illuminating all our borrowed faces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem that feels assembled through cut-up and copy-paste techniques, blending museum observations, social anxiety, financial hardship, artistic frustration, and avant-garde music into grammatically unstable yet vivid imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
At the museum, every white wall had already forgiven itself. PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH, said the small brass weather. I kept my hands inside my coat, where the rent was overdue and a grocery receipt curled like a dead fern. In Gallery 6, a saint held his own head beneath one arm, very practical, very composed. I understood this as a budget.

People moved around me with the soft confidence of captions. Oil on panel. Gift of an anonymous donor. Linen, blood, probable workshop. I practiced my face in the glass: interested but not hungry, alone but not abandoned, thirty-seven cents accumulating interest in the republic of my pocket. Someone laughed near the Cubists and all my bones rearranged into exits.

COPY / PASTE: horse, staircase, mother’s voicemail, declined. COPY / PASTE: blue square where a window should be. The artist has investigated absence since 1998. I have investigated it since Tuesday. My notebook refuses the commission; each sentence arrives wearing another sentence’s shoes. I draw a line. The line files for bankruptcy. I draw a bird. The bird resembles a late fee.

From the headphones: bass clarinet chewing through a locked room, prepared piano full of screws and weather, one violin climbing a ladder made of alarms. Then silence, professionally amplified. Then a woman whispering the inventory of a demolished kitchen: one cup / no handle / one father / intermittent / three spoons / enormous dusk. I nod as if this is music, as if nodding is not my oldest disguise.

In the café, coffee costs the amount I have reserved for becoming someone. I order water and sit beside a sculpture of stacked fluorescent tubes, their electric stutter saying NOW NOW NOT NOW. Across the atrium, beautiful strangers network beneath a mobile of aluminum knives. Their names attach cleanly to their bodies. Mine keeps buffering.

Museum closes in fifteen minutes. Museum closes inside my chest. Guards gather the remaining light with black gloves. The saint returns his head to the dark. I leave through the gift shop without purchasing the postcard of the painting I failed to make, while outside the city performs its twelve-tone siren, its bus-brake percussion, its coins-in-a-cup coda—and I, unauthorized reproduction, walk home under a sky pasted crookedly over everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
